lede: Blood is a liquid carrying four kinds of cargo, pushed round the body through three kinds of tube. Which cargo, and which tube, is most of what B2 asks about the circulatory system.
can: Name the four components of blood and give the function of each one.
Give three adaptations of a red blood cell, and say what the plasma carries.
Match an artery, a vein and a capillary to the job each one does.

text: Blood components, cell lysis and blood vessels

md: Spin a tube of blood in a centrifuge and it splits into two: a straw-coloured liquid on top, a dark red sludge underneath. Everything blood does is done by one of the four things in those two layers — and by the three kinds of tube that carry them around.

md:
**Red cells** carry the oxygen. **White cells** defend against disease. **Platelets** convert **fibrinogen** into **fibrin**, the mesh that makes blood clot and a scab form. **Plasma** carries all of them, plus food molecules, carbon dioxide, hormones and urea.

Notice what plasma does **not** carry: oxygen. Almost all of it travels inside the red cells.

prompt: Which of these is NOT transported by the plasma?
explain: Oxygen. It is bound to haemoglobin inside the red blood cells, which is why 'oxygen' is on the reject list for this question.

text: 2. A cell built for one job

alt: A field of view down a microscope showing dozens of round, purple-stained red blood cells packed closely together, each with a distinctly paler centre, and two small dark-stained specks between them.
credit: U.S. Air Force photo/Airman 1st Class Laura Max., Wikimedia Commons, Public domain
caption: A real smear. The pale centre of each cell is the dip in the middle of the disc; the two dark specks are platelets.
prompt: Why does each red cell look paler in the middle than round the edge — and which adaptation does that pale centre show you?

md: A red blood cell is a **biconcave** disc: dimpled on both sides, which is why the middle of each one looks paler under a microscope. That shape gives a **large surface area** for absorbing oxygen. The cell has **no nucleus**, which leaves more room inside, and it is packed with **haemoglobin**, the pigment that contains **iron** and binds the oxygen.

prompt: The shape of a red blood cell is described by one word: ______.
explain: Biconcave. 'Round' and 'flat' are not credited, and Summer 2025 examiners found fewer candidates gave this word than gave 'nucleus'.

title: Why the plant cell survives and this one does not
md:
Put either cell in pure water and water floods in by osmosis — the cytoplasm is more concentrated than the water outside. A plant cell has a **cell wall** that will not stretch, so it stops taking water in once it is turgid.

A red blood cell has **only a membrane**. Nothing limits the water, so it swells until the membrane splits. That bursting has a name: **lysis**.

prompt: Why does a red blood cell burst in pure water when a plant cell does not?
options: It has no cell wall to limit the entry of water
Its membrane is not permeable to water
answer: It has no cell wall to limit the entry of water
explain: The wall is the whole difference. The missing nucleus has nothing to do with it.

text: 4. A worked answer, start to finish

title: GCSE Biology Revision "The Blood"
why: A short second pass over the four components, now that you have met them.

title: Worked example: 'A drawing of a red blood cell is 42 mm across; the real cell is 7 µm across. Calculate the magnification. [3]'
md:
**Step 1 — same unit.** 42 mm × 1000 = **42000 µm**. You cannot divide millimetres by micrometres any more than you can divide miles by inches.
**Step 2 — the equation.** magnification = drawn size ÷ real size = 42000 ÷ 7.
**Step 3 — the answer.** **×6000**, with no unit: a magnification is a ratio of two lengths.

prompt: Your turn. A second drawing of the same 7 µm cell measures 21 mm across. What is its magnification? Give the number only.
explain: 21 mm is 21 000 µm, and 21 000 ÷ 7 = 3000. Convert first, divide second.

md:
**Artery** — thick wall with **muscle and elastic fibres**, small lumen. It carries blood **away from the heart** at high pressure, and the elastic fibres stretch and recoil with every beat.
**Vein** — thin wall, **large lumen**, and **valves**. It carries blood back **towards the heart** at low pressure.
**Capillary** — wall **one cell thick** and **permeable**, so materials are exchanged with the tissues.

prompt: Which vessel has the thickest wall and the smallest lumen?
explain: The artery. High pressure needs a thick wall, and the wall takes up the room the lumen might have had.

alt: A vein shown twice. On the left, blood flowing towards the heart pushes two valve flaps back against the wall. On the right, blood starting to flow backwards fills the flaps so they meet in the middle and close the tube.

Muscles around the vein squeeze it, and the valves</text><text x="40" y="300" font-size="11.5">stop the blood sliding backwards between squeezes. Arteries have no valves: the heart supplies the pressure.</text></g></svg>
caption: Open with the flow, shut against it.

md:
By the time blood reaches a vein it has been through a whole capillary bed, and the pressure is low. It is pushed along by the muscles around the vein squeezing it — and between squeezes it could easily slide back.

The valves fill and shut when that happens, so blood can only travel **towards the heart**. An artery needs no valves: the heart keeps the pressure high enough that the blood never goes backwards.

prompt: Valves in a vein stop the blood flowing ______.
explain: Backwards. The word the scheme wants is backflow, or 'they maintain the direction of flow'.

title: You can now…

md:
Name the four components of blood and the job of each.
Say what a red cell gave up, and what that bought it.
Tell the three vessels apart by their walls and their work.
Say why only veins need valves.

Blood often opens the Foundation paper: a matching exercise worth three, then single marks for the nucleus, the biconcave shape and iron, and one for a substance in the plasma. Vessels come as a tick table worth up to six, and again beside the heart question. Cell lysis is Higher only. Stuck: name the component and give its one job.
